title: Asita's tears, in verse
hookLine: the sage weeps that he will not hear the child teach (Buddhacarita 1)

lines: A HOLY MAN NOBODY SENT FOR.
cards: A palace celebrating a new baby, and a guest nobody sent for: an old holy man, Asita, who has seen signs and come on his own. The king receives him with honor and brings out the child. Asita looks for a long time.
And his eyes fill, and the tears run down. In a room like that, a holy man weeping over a newborn seems to mean only one thing. Year one met Asita in a few lines.
The poem gives the scene room, and lets both men speak: a frightened father, and an old man who has to explain his tears.

teach.b: First, the king's fear. King Shuddhodana sees the tears and trembles. Is my son's life short, he asks; is some harm coming to him?
It is the question a parent asks. Second, Asita's answer.
Not for the child, he says. The child is well, and more than well. He will leave the kingdom behind, wake up, and teach a way out of suffering for the world.
In the poem's image, paraphrased here, the teaching will be like a boat that carries people across a great flood. Third, the turn. Then why weep?
Because I am old, Asita says. My time is nearly over.

teach.h: I WON'T LIVE TO HEAR HIM.
teach.b: This child will teach, and I won't be alive to hear it. The tears are for himself. He arrived at the right house, too early in the story.
He doesn't resent the child or pretend not to care. He weeps honestly, and he blesses what he won't share. And fourth, the shadow.

teach.h: THE BOY WILL LEAVE THE KINGDOM.
teach.b: In front of the king, Asita has said the boy will leave the kingdom.
A father who wanted an heir has just heard he may be raising a wanderer, and that sentence will sit in the palace for years.
Some people know a version of Asita's grief: a grandparent who won't see the wedding, a founder who won't see the school finished. His answer is to love it anyway, from where he stands.

how: Asita's visit is told in other Buddhist texts besides this poem, and it appears in paintings and carvings of the Buddha's early life.

o: a sage weeping because the newborn will die young
a sage weeping because he won't live to hear the child
a mother's tears at her son's leaving home

p: asks if his son is in danger
a boat across a great flood
for himself, not for the child

s: Asita weeps because he sees danger for the child
he tells the king the child is well; he weeps because he won't live to hear him teach.
Asita tells the king the boy will leave the kingdom
the sage foretells a life of awakening and teaching, not the throne.
in the poem the sage comes on his own, drawn by signs.

games.q: you're King Shuddhodana. an old holy man holds your newborn son and starts to weep. what do you do?
o: thank him for his blessing and move on.
ask him straight out whether your son is in danger.
have him shown out of the palace.
games.why: the king trembles and asks if harm is coming. Asita answers that the child is well. the tears are for himself.

practice: Bring to mind a teacher you'll never meet: a writer long gone, a grandparent's grandparent whose sayings got passed down, or someone not yet born who will teach what you can't.
Let that person sit in the room with you; you don't have to say anything. Just let there be gratitude, and a little of Asita's ache, side by side.

wordCard.voice: Asita's tears. An old sage weeps over the newborn, not from fear for the child, but because he won't live to hear him teach. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: born too early. An old man's tears, and a blessing. Day six hundred ninety-nine.
